title: Move SQLAlchemy session.query to 2.0-style select
summary: Port the legacy Query API to select and session.scalars, fix the Row objects that execute hands back, then use execute on purpose for a join with the team name.

files.content:
from datetime import datetime

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Team(Base):
    __tablename__ = "teams"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]


class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str]
    name: Mapped[str]
    is_active: Mapped[bool]
    created_at: Mapped[datetime]
    team_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("teams.id"))
    team: Mapped[Team] = relationship()

turns.user: the SQLAlchemy 2.0 docs call session.query legacy. can you move users.py to the new style

assistant.body: Sure! In 2.0 style you build the query with select() and hand it to the Session to run. When you want ORM entities back, use session.scalars. When a single value comes back, like an aggregate, use session.scalar. filter becomes where, and count() becomes func.count().

turns.user: admin list page now throws AttributeError: name. it's active_users

assistant.body: Apologies, my previous answer was incorrect. active_users was the one place I used session.execute. execute returns Row objects. Even for select(User), each Row is a tuple holding one User, so you would need row.User.name rather than user.name. scalars takes the first column of each Row and gives you the User itself.

turns.user: fixed. also want the team name in the list. no N+1 please

assistant.body: Now, this is where execute is the right call. select(User, Team.name) picks two columns, a User and a string, and join(User.team) keeps it to one SQL statement. With two columns, scalars would throw Team.name away. Taking each Row from execute as a tuple lets you unpack it into user and team_name. I left active_users as it was, for separation of concerns.

from .models import Team, User


def active_users_with_team(session: Session) -> list[tuple[User, str]]:
    stmt = (
        select(User, Team.name)
        .join(User.team)
        .where(User.is_active)
        .order_by(User.created_at)
    )
    return [(user, team_name) for user, team_name in session.execute(stmt)]
